title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 24
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A hairdressing chain introduced online booking and reports that the proportion of appointments missed fell from 14 per cent to 6 per cent. It concludes that online booking makes customers more reliable.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some customers still book by telephone.
B. Online bookings require a card to be registered, and the chain now charges a fee for a missed appointment.
C. The chain has salons in twelve towns.
D. Stylists prefer the new system.
E. Bookings can be made up to three months ahead.
questions.explanation: A penalty introduced alongside the channel is sufficient to explain the change, and it is the penalty rather than the booking method that alters the incentive.

questions.prompt: A mobile network installed additional masts in a rural county and reports that customer complaints about coverage fell by half. It concludes that coverage has improved.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the masts cost to install
B. Whether residents objected to the masts
C. Whether measured signal strength across the county changed over the same period
D. How many customers the network has in the county
E. Whether competitors also installed masts
questions.explanation: Complaints depend on reporting effort and expectation as well as on signal; a direct measure settles what the proxy cannot.

questions.prompt: A campsite introduced a two-night minimum stay and reports that its occupancy rate rose. The owner concludes that guests prefer longer stays.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The campsite has forty pitches.
B. Some guests stay a week.
C. Occupancy is measured across the season.
D. The site is busiest in August.
E. The rule eliminated single-night bookings that had left pitches empty on adjacent nights, so the same guests now fill more nights without anyone's preference having changed.
questions.explanation: The rule changes what can be booked rather than what anyone wants; the occupancy gain is a scheduling effect.

questions.prompt: A wine shop notes that customers who accept a tasting sample buy more expensive bottles than those who decline, and plans to offer a sample to every customer in order to raise average spending.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Customers who intend to buy something special are the ones who stop for a tasting, while those buying an everyday bottle decline in order to leave quickly.
B. Samples cost the shop money.
C. The shop offers tastings on Saturdays.
D. Some customers buy more than one bottle.
E. Tastings are conducted by trained staff.
questions.explanation: The sample marks an intention that already exists, so offering it universally need not raise spending among those who were never going to browse.

questions.prompt: Every property maintained by the Ellery estate that has cast-iron guttering is inspected twice a year. No property inspected twice a year suffered water damage last winter. Some properties maintained by the estate suffered water damage last winter.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Cast-iron guttering prevents water damage.
B. Most properties are inspected twice a year.
C. No inspected property will ever suffer damage.
D. Some properties maintained by the estate do not have cast-iron guttering.
E. Damaged properties are older than the others.
questions.explanation: Damaged properties are not inspected twice yearly, and cast-iron guttering implies such inspection, so those properties have other guttering.

questions.prompt: A hospital changed its catering supplier and reports that the weight of food waste from patient meals has fallen by a third. Managers describe this as evidence that patients prefer the new meals.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of the new contract
B. does not distinguish between wards
C. assumes waste measures preference, when smaller portions would produce the same fall
D. relies on a single measure of weight
E. overlooks meals brought in by visitors
questions.explanation: Less food served produces less food wasted; without portion size held constant the measure cannot support a claim about preference.

questions.prompt: A school reports that pupils who attend its optional residential trip achieve better results in the following year, and proposes to make the trip compulsory in order to raise attainment.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the proposal?
options: A. Attendance requires a parental contribution, and the pupils who attend are those whose families can pay and are already the higher-attaining group.
B. The trip lasts four days.
C. Staff volunteer to supervise the trip.
D. The trip includes outdoor activities.
E. Some pupils attend similar trips elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The attendance filter is income and prior attainment, so the association need reflect nothing the trip does.

questions.prompt: A delivery company that pays cyclists per parcel reports that its couriers deliver more parcels per hour than couriers at a rival paying by the hour. It concludes that piece rates raise productivity.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The company's couriers use their own bicycles.
B. Parcels are of similar size at both firms.
C. The rival pays slightly more per hour.
D. The company assigns its couriers dense city-centre rounds while the rival's couriers cover outer suburbs.
E. Both firms deliver on weekdays only.
questions.explanation: Round density determines parcels per hour far more than payment method, so the comparison is between territories rather than between pay systems.

questions.prompt: A hotel added a gym and reports that guests who use it rate their stay more highly than guests who do not. Management concludes that the gym has improved guest satisfaction.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The gym is open at all hours.
B. Ratings from guests who did not use the gym also rose after it opened, and the rise coincided with the opening at each of the four hotels where it was installed in different months.
C. The gym equipment was expensive.
D. Some guests use gyms elsewhere in the city.
E. The hotel advertises the gym on its website.
questions.explanation: It removes the self-selection and ties the change to the opening across several sites at different times, which is close to a staggered design.

questions.prompt: A group of farms bought a combine harvester jointly and reports that each farm's machinery costs fell by 40 per cent. An adviser recommends joint purchase to all farms in the district.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the recommendation as a general one?
options: A. The harvester required a shared maintenance agreement.
B. Joint purchase requires a written agreement.
C. The harvester was bought second-hand.
D. Some farms in the district are larger than those in the group.
E. The farms that shared successfully harvest crops that ripen at different times, while most farms in the district grow the same crop and would need the machine in the same fortnight.
questions.explanation: The saving depends on staggered demand; where every farm needs the machine at once, sharing fails precisely when the machine is needed.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a community energy scheme argue that local ownership of a wind turbine will reduce residents' electricity bills. A critic replies that the turbine will sell its output into the national market at the prevailing price, like any other generator.
questions.question: The critic's reply is best understood as
options: A. denying that the turbine will generate electricity
B. arguing that wind generation is unreliable
C. pointing out that the benefit to residents comes as a share of revenue rather than as cheaper supply
D. objecting to the cost of the turbine
E. claiming that residents will not support the scheme
questions.explanation: The reply concedes the scheme may pay residents while denying the mechanism claimed, which is a distinction between a dividend and a discount on supply.

questions.passageText:
Firms that can show half their customers one version of a page and half another have acquired something rare in business: the ability to run a controlled experiment on a decision that would otherwise be settled by argument. The method has been transformative, and the enthusiasm for it has outrun the understanding of what it establishes.

The first limit is the outcome measured. An experiment answers a question about the quantity it counts, typically over the days it runs. A change that raises purchases this week may raise returns next month or reduce the likelihood that a customer comes back, and neither effect appears in the test that declared the change a success. Firms that test heavily on short-run metrics accumulate changes that were each locally justified.

The second is the population. The result holds for the customers who saw the test, at that moment, under those conditions. Where the tested change interacts with something seasonal, or with a promotion running simultaneously, the estimate is specific to circumstances that will not recur.

The third is statistical and the most easily abused. Running many tests guarantees that some will produce apparently significant results by chance, and a firm that tests continuously and acts on whichever comparison crosses a threshold will implement a steady stream of nothing. Disciplined practice fixes the metric and the duration in advance, and treats a surprising result as a reason to repeat the test rather than to ship the change — which is a much slower way to work than the method's reputation implies.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a change that raises purchases in a week-long test may nonetheless
options: A. reduce the number of customers who see it
B. raise returns later or reduce the likelihood that customers come back
C. fail to reach statistical significance
D. be impossible to implement
E. produce identical results in a repeat test
questions.explanation: Neither of those effects appears in a test that measured short-run purchases and declared success.

questions.passageText:
The international agreement that phased out ozone-depleting chemicals is the most successful environmental treaty yet concluded, and the reasons for its success are frequently misidentified as evidence that international cooperation is straightforward when the science is clear.

The science was not initially clear. The mechanism was proposed a decade before the Antarctic hole was observed, and the observation itself was so far outside expectation that automated processing had been discarding the readings as errors. What made action possible was not certainty but a combination of features the climate problem lacks.

The substances involved were produced by a small number of firms, which made monitoring feasible and negotiation manageable. Substitutes existed or could be developed within years rather than decades, so compliance did not require abandoning an activity, only changing an input. The harm was vivid, personal and easy to describe. And the costs of compliance fell mainly on the same wealthy countries that had produced the substances, so the distributional argument that dominates climate negotiation was comparatively muted — and where it did arise, a fund to assist developing countries was agreed and used.

The treaty also improved over time, tightening its schedules as evidence accumulated, which is a design feature rather than an accident. The lesson is not that treaties work when science is settled. It is that this problem had a structure — few producers, available substitutes, concentrated costs, legible harm — that made a solution reachable, and that a problem lacking those features will not be solved by the same instrument merely because the science is at least as good.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that at the time the ozone agreement was negotiated, the science was
options: A. fully settled and universally accepted
B. disputed by the firms that produced the substances
C. based entirely on laboratory work
D. less advanced than climate science is now
E. not initially clear, with the key observation initially discarded as error
questions.explanation: The mechanism preceded the observation by a decade, and automated processing had been rejecting the readings.

questions.passageText:
Building a transport link to a poorer region in order to develop it is among the most durable ideas in regional policy, and its record is mixed in a way that is instructive rather than discouraging.

A new link reduces the cost of moving goods and people in both directions. That is the point, and it is also the difficulty: a region connected to a larger economy becomes cheaper to serve from outside as well as cheaper to export from. Where local firms were protected by distance, the connection exposes them to competition they may not survive, and studies of new motorways and high-speed lines have found activity relocating toward the larger centre in some cases and toward the smaller in others.

Which occurs depends on what the smaller region already has. Where it holds a genuine advantage — lower costs, a specialised workforce, land — connection lets that advantage be exploited. Where its firms existed only because reaching them from elsewhere was expensive, connection removes the reason for their existence.

The policy implication is not that links should not be built. It is that a transport link is a multiplier rather than a source: it amplifies whatever a place's underlying position already is. A region with nothing to sell does not acquire something by being reached more quickly, and the schemes that disappointed most reliably were those in which the link was the whole of the strategy rather than a component of one.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a new transport link creates difficulty for a poorer region because it
options: A. raises the cost of local production
B. attracts workers away from local firms
C. requires local authorities to borrow
D. makes the region cheaper to serve from outside as well as cheaper to export from
E. reduces the value of land
questions.explanation: The two-way reduction in transport cost is the point and the problem, exposing firms protected by distance.

questions.passageText:
A legal system that decides cases by reference to earlier decisions appears at first to prize consistency above justice: a court is bound by what other courts held, including where it thinks them mistaken. The justification is more interesting than the appearance suggests.

Precedent does three things. It makes conduct predictable, so that people can arrange their affairs knowing how a dispute would be resolved. It constrains judicial discretion, requiring reasons that connect to what has been decided before rather than to a judge's preference. And it distributes labour across time, since a question settled need not be reargued in every case.

The system is less rigid than it looks, because what binds is not the outcome but the reasoning necessary to it, and identifying that is itself an argument. A later court that considers an earlier decision wrong can distinguish it by identifying a material difference in facts, and the practice of distinguishing does much of the work that formal overruling would do more visibly. This is a genuine flexibility and a genuine weakness: a rule can be eroded by distinctions until little remains, without anyone stating that it has changed.

The deeper tension is that predictability is itself a component of justice rather than a rival to it. A rule announced after the fact cannot guide anyone, and a system that reached the best result in each case by its own lights, unconstrained by what it had held before, would be one under which nobody could know what the law required — which is a defect of a different kind, and one the case-by-case view tends not to price.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what binds a later court is
options: A. the outcome of the earlier case
B. the seniority of the earlier court alone
C. the reasoning necessary to the earlier decision
D. the parties' agreement
E. the statute under which the case arose
questions.explanation: The passage notes that identifying that reasoning is itself an argument, which is where the flexibility enters.

The system is less rigid than it looks, because what binds is not the outcome but the reasoning necessary to it, and identifying that is itself an argument. A later court that considers an earlier decision wrong can distinguish it by identifying a material difference in facts, and the practice of distinguishing does much of the work that formal overruling would do more visibly. This is a genuine flexibility and a genuine weakness: a rule can be eroded by distinctions until little remains, without anyone stating that it has changed.

The deeper tension is that predictability is itself a component of justice rather than a rival to it. A rule announced after the fact cannot guide anyone, and a system that reached the best result in each case by its own lights, unconstrained by what it had held before, would be one under which nobody could know what the law required — which is a defect of a different kind, and one the case-by-case view tends not to price.
